intro.html: Stories are full of tricksters: the fake doctor with a miracle tonic, the stranger who claims to be someone he is not, the schemer who plots in secret. This topic gives you exact words for each kind of trick and for the people who help.

Tricksters: a charlatan fakes a skill; an impostor fakes who he is; a wily person is good at tricks. Tricks: a ruse, subterfuge, chicanery, a machination. Partners in a wrong: collusion, complicit, connive.
Several of these words carry Latin pictures inside them: subterfuge is fleeing in secret, collusion is playing together, and connive is shutting your eyes.

words.ex: The {wily} fox waited until the farmer fell asleep, then slipped under the fence.
words.ctx: The chess champion was {wily}: she pretended to make a careless move, then sprang a trap that won the game three turns later.
words.etym: From wile, an old word for a sly trick.

mn.text: While the guard dog snores, the fox tiptoes off with an egg; he plans his tricks for just that moment, because he is {wily}.

labels.text: WHILE he sleeps: a WILY fox

scene.alt: A sly fox tiptoes off with an egg while the guard dog sleeps and a hen looks shocked.

words.def: a fake who claims special knowledge or skill in order to fool people
words.ex: The {charlatan} sold bottles of colored water as a cure for baldness.
words.ctx: He called himself a famous healer, but he was a {charlatan}: he had never studied medicine, and his “miracle tonic” was only sugar water.
words.etym: From Italian ciarlatano, “a quack,” a seller of fake cures.

mn.text: Charlie sells a “magic tonic” from his cart that he swears will make you fly; a man who claims a skill he does not have is a {charlatan}.

scene.alt: A man in a top hat holds up a bottle of “magic tonic” while a doubtful old man and a girl look on.

words.def: a person who pretends to be someone else to fool others
words.ex: The man at the door claimed to be from the water company, but he was an {impostor} with a fake badge.
words.ctx: Everyone believed the stranger was the old captain’s long-lost nephew until a neighbor who knew the family arrived and exposed him as an {impostor}.
words.etym: From Late Latin impostor, “a deceiver,” from imponere, “to put upon, to impose on (someone).”

mn.text: Rex puts on a chef’s hat and a fake mustache and poses as the famous Chef Sven, until the real Sven walks in; Rex is an {impostor}.

scene.alt: A sneaky man in a chef’s hat and fake mustache claims to be Chef Sven as the real chef points at him.

words.def: a trick meant to fool someone
words.ex: The phone call about a free cruise was a {ruse} to get our bank number.
words.ctx: The “quick stop at the dentist” was only a {ruse}; when we pulled into the lot, all my friends jumped out from behind the cars to shout “Happy birthday!”
words.etym: From French ruse, which first meant the doubling back of a hunted animal to throw off the hounds.

mn.text: Rex offers Pip a lovely rose, but it is a joke flower that squirts water in his face; the gift was a {ruse}.

scene.alt: A man offers a boy a flower that squirts water in his face.

words.def: a sly trick used to hide something or to get out of something
words.ex: Pretending to be asleep was the twins’ favorite {subterfuge} for skipping chores.
words.ctx: Unable to leave the dull party openly, Felix turned to {subterfuge}: he had a friend call him with a made-up emergency so he could slip out early.
words.etym: From Late Latin subterfugium, from subterfugere, “to escape secretly”: subter- (beneath, secretly) + fugere (to flee).

mn.text: Pip tucks a pillow under his blanket so it looks like he is asleep, then sneaks off to play; the pillow is his {subterfuge}.

scene.alt: A boy sneaks out the door with a ball while a pillow under his blanket pretends to be him asleep.

words.def: clever, dishonest trickery, especially in business or law
words.ex: The card game was pure {chicanery}; the dealer had marked every ace.
words.ctx: The contract looked fair, but it was full of {chicanery}: tiny print on the last page let the company raise the price whenever it liked.
words.etym: From French chicanerie, from chicaner (to quibble, to argue over small points).

mn.text: Sly Victor paints a plain hen gold and swears she lays golden eggs; that kind of dishonest selling is {chicanery}.

scene.alt: A sly seller points to a hen he has painted gold, while a doubtful buyer scratches his head.

words.def: a secret, crafty plot, usually meant to do harm
words.ex: Despite all her rival’s {machinations}, Lila won the spelling bee fair and square.
words.ctx: The king’s adviser smiled at court every day, but behind closed doors his {machinations} never stopped: he forged letters, bribed guards and plotted to seize the throne.
words.etym: From Latin machinatio, “a contrivance, a plot,” from machinari (to devise, to plot), from machina (machine).
words.note: Say it with a hard k: mak-uh-NAY-shun, like the start of mackerel.

mn.text: In his secret lab, Rex builds a giant machine with gears and levers, all to steal the town’s pie-contest trophy; his crafty plot is a {machination}.

scene.alt: A sneaky man in a lab coat plots beside gears, a robot and a board that reads “steal trophy.”

words.def: secret teamwork for a dishonest purpose
words.ex: The two bakeries were caught in {collusion}, secretly agreeing to raise their prices on the same day.
words.ctx: The referee’s strange calls were no accident; an inquiry found {collusion} between him and a coach who had promised him part of the prize money.
words.etym: From Latin collusio, from colludere, “to play together, to be in secret league”: com- (together) + ludere (to play).

mn.cue: COL + LUD: PLAYING TOGETHER in secret
mn.text: Two players on rival teams secretly agree who will win and split the prize; their dishonest teamwork is {collusion}.

scene.alt: Two players from rival teams whisper and pass a secret deal on the field.

words.def: taking part with others in doing something wrong
words.ex: By hiding his friend’s copy of the stolen answers, Jonah became {complicit} in the cheating.
words.ctx: The guard did not take the painting himself, but he was {complicit}: he left the back door unlocked and looked the other way.
words.etym: From complicity, which goes back to Latin complicare, “to fold together.”

mn.text: Kai does not take the cookies himself, but he holds the ladder while Pip climbs to the jar; as Pip’s accomplice, Kai is {complicit}.

scene.alt: One boy holds a ladder steady while another climbs up toward the cookie jar.

words.def: to plot secretly, or to let a wrong happen by looking away
words.ex: The two brothers {connived} to sneak the stray puppy into the house without their parents noticing.
words.ctx: The night guard {connived} at the theft: he watched the thieves on his camera screen, then shut his eyes and said nothing.
words.etym: From Latin connivere, “to shut the eyes,” and so to pretend not to see.
words.note: To connive at a wrong is to let it happen on purpose; to connive with someone is to plot together.

mn.cue: CON + NIVE: shut your eyes to a CON
mn.text: The museum guard covers his eyes while Rex tiptoes past with the jewel; by pretending not to see, the guard {connives} at the theft.

scene.alt: A guard covers his eyes on purpose while a thief tiptoes past with a jewel.

after.cap: Tricksters, their tricks, and the people who help them.

after.html: Two pairs to keep straight: collusion (secret teamwork) is not collision (a crash), and a charlatan fakes a skill, while an impostor fakes an identity.

items.q: A stranger arrives using the new doctor’s name and wearing her badge. He is best called an…
items.why: He is pretending to be a particular person, so he is an impostor. A charlatan fakes a skill, not an identity.

items.q: The two shops secretly agreed to charge the same high price. This was…
items.why: Secret teamwork for a dishonest purpose is collusion. A collision is a crash.

items.q: True or false: machination is usually said with a hard k sound: mak-uh-NAY-shun.
items.why: True. The ch sounds like the k in mechanic, not the sh in machine.

items.q: True or false: to connive can mean to pretend not to see a wrong so that it can happen.
items.why: True. The Latin connivere means to shut the eyes. To connive at a theft is to let it happen on purpose.
